theory.title: Firewalls and Ports
theory.recap: You can read routing tables and pick the most specific route. Now your packet also carries a port number, and gateways check that port. The path opens with R1 - longest-prefix match, just like before - and the new mechanic only appears once you've routed correctly.
theory.plainObjective: Route through R1 to reach the firewall fork, then pass through the gate that allows your port (80).
theory.summary: Every server on the internet sits behind a firewall with rules like these. When your browser connects to a website, the request only gets through because port 80 or 443 is explicitly allowed.

bodyParagraphs.heading: What is a port?
bodyParagraphs.text: Every network service listens on a numbered port. Web servers use port 80 (HTTP) or 443 (HTTPS). SSH remote access uses port 22. Your packet carries port 80 because it is HTTP traffic - the destination IP gets you to the right machine, the port gets you to the right service on it.

bodyParagraphs.heading: What does a firewall do?
bodyParagraphs.text: A firewall sits between network segments and checks each packet against a list of rules. Rules specify which ports are allowed or denied. The first matching rule wins. If no rule matches, traffic is denied by default.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Routing comes first
bodyParagraphs.text: R1 still uses the rules from Act I: match the destination IP against the routing table, longest prefix wins. Only once R1 sends you to the firewall fork does the new port-filtering rule apply.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Reading the rules
bodyParagraphs.text: Each firewall gate shows what it allows. One reads ALLOWS: 80, 443 and the other ALLOWS: 22. Your packet carries port 80, so only one gate will let you through.

theory.mission:
You carry HTTP traffic on port 80, destined for 10.0.2.20.

R1 has three overlapping routes - pick the most specific one to the destination subnet. After R1, choose the firewall gate that allows port 80.

termIntroductions.headline: Port
termIntroductions.body: A port is a number that identifies which service a packet is addressed to. You carry port 80 - the standard port for HTTP web traffic. Think of it as the apartment number inside a building whose street address is the IP.

termIntroductions.headline: Firewall
termIntroductions.body: A firewall checks every packet against a set of rules before letting it through. Rules are matched top to bottom - the first match wins. If nothing matches, the packet is dropped. Read the labels on the gates ahead.

termIntroductions.headline: HTTP
termIntroductions.body: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is how web browsers fetch pages. It runs on port 80. When you type a URL, your browser sends an HTTP request - a packet just like you - toward port 80 on a web server.
